content: The disease burden of Taenia solium cysticercosis in Cameroon was studied by Praet et al. in 2009, highlighting its significant impact on public health. Ndimbuanzi PC et al. conducted a systematic review in 2010 focusing on the frequency of neurocysticercosis, particularly in individuals with epilepsy, emphasizing the neurological complications associated with this parasitic infection. Brooker S et al. explored the epidemiology of single and multiple species of helminth infections among schoolchildren in Busia District, Kenya, in 2000, revealing the widespread prevalence of these infections in endemic regions. Faulkner H et al. in 2005 examined the associations between filarial and gastrointestinal nematodes, providing insights into co-infections and their interactions. Canning D in 2006 discussed priority setting for neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), emphasizing the need for integrated approaches to address these diseases. Hotez PJ et al. in 2006 proposed incorporating a rapid-impact package for NTDs alongside programs for HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis, and malaria, advocating for a synergistic approach to global health challenges. Chan M addressed the WHO global partners meeting on NTDs in 2012, underscoring the importance of collaborative efforts in combating these diseases. Mwangi TW, Bethony JM, and Brooker S in 2006 examined the interactions between malaria and helminths in humans, providing an epidemiological perspective on co-infections. Nacher M in 2004 reviewed the interactions between worm infections and malaria, highlighting the complex interplay between these diseases. Supali T et al. in 2010 investigated polyparasitism and its impact on the immune system, shedding light on the immunological consequences of multiple parasitic infections. The WHO Global Health Observatory Map Gallery in 2011 provided a visual representation of NTDs, facilitating better understanding and planning for disease control. Colley DG and Secor WE in 2007 outlined a research agenda for schistosomiasis, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. Dujardin JC et al. in 2010 identified research priorities for neglected infectious diseases in Latin America and the Caribbean, focusing on region-specific challenges. The WHO informal consultation in 2009 addressed foodborne trematode infections and taeniasis/cysticercosis, providing recommendations for control strategies. A workshop in Brazil in 2008 focused on research priorities for schistosomiasis, emphasizing the importance of local and regional efforts. Guyatt HL et al. in 2001 evaluated the efficacy of school-based anthelmintic treatments against anemia in Tanzanian children, demonstrating the benefits of deworming programs. Brooker S et al. in 2008 analyzed the cost and cost-effectiveness of nationwide school-based helminth control in Uganda, highlighting the economic implications of scaling up interventions. Kabatereine NB et al. in 2007 assessed the impact of a national helminth control program on infection and morbidity among Ugandan schoolchildren, showcasing the success of large-scale deworming efforts. Ramzy RM et al. in 2006 evaluated the effect of annual mass drug administration with diethylcarbamazine and albendazole on bancroftian filariasis in Egypt, providing a comprehensive assessment of its impact. Lindblade KA et al. in 2007 documented the elimination of Onchocerca volvulus transmission in Guatemala, demonstrating the feasibility of eradication efforts. Vieira JC et al. in 2007 examined the long-term impact of ivermectin treatment on onchocerciasis in Ecuador, highlighting its potential for eliminating infection. Rodríguez-Pérez MA et al. in 2008 provided evidence for the suppression of Onchocerca volvulus transmission in Mexico, showcasing the success of targeted interventions. Diawara L et al. in 2009 demonstrated the feasibility of onchocerciasis elimination with ivermectin treatment in endemic foci in Africa, presenting evidence from studies in Mali and Senegal. Little MP et al. in 2004 analyzed the incidence of blindness during the Onchocerciasis Control Programme in West Africa, emphasizing the program's success in reducing disease burden. French MD et al. in 2010 observed a reduction in Schistosoma mansoni transmission following large-scale praziquantel administration in Uganda, using mathematical modeling to predict outcomes. The WHO Technical Report Series in 2012 outlined research priorities for helminth infections, providing a roadmap for future studies. Kolaczinski JH et al. in 2007 discussed the prospects and challenges of integrated control for NTDs in Uganda, emphasizing the need for coordinated efforts. Utzinger J et al. in 2009 advocated for integrated and sustainable control of schistosomiasis and other NTDs, while cautioning against potential pitfalls. Ramaiah KD et al. in 2000 evaluated a program to eliminate lymphatic filariasis in Tamil Nadu, India, focusing on compliance with annual single-dose DEC mass treatment. They also reported in 2009 on the prolonged persistence of residual Wuchereria bancrofti infection after cessation of a DEC-fortified salt program. Brady MA, Hooper PJ, and Ottesen EA in 2006 projected the benefits of integrating NTD programs in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the potential for cost-effective interventions. Brooker S and Utzinger J in 2007 emphasized the importance of integrated disease mapping in addressing polyparasitism. Bethony J et al. in 2006 reviewed soil-transmitted helminth infections, including ascariasis, trichuriasis, and hookworm, providing a comprehensive overview of their global impact. Sousa-Figueiredo JC et al. in 2009 assessed morbidity associated with urinary schistosomiasis, using urinary albumin levels and tract pathologies as indicators. Vivas-Martinez S et al. in 1998 studied onchocerciasis in southern Venezuela, identifying altitude and blackfly species composition as predictors of endemicity. Botto C et al. in 2005 examined geographical patterns of onchocerciasis in Venezuela, exploring the relationship between environment and infection prevalence. Brooker S et al. in 2009 updated an atlas of human helminth infections, using East Africa as an example to demonstrate the utility of geospatial health tools.
